messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Dancer
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 58

He is a 41-year-old Middle Eastern man who comes to the work carrying himself with a kind of careful control, as if he has learned to conserve every movement. He is married, a dancer by profession, and he speaks about the body the way some people speak about weather: as something powerful, beautiful, and sometimes dangerous. Before the war, dance is the place where he feels most like himself. It is how he earns money, how he connects to his culture, and how he has always understood discipline, grace, and belonging.

The trauma begins in his city, during a period when violence has become ordinary enough that people stop asking whether the next explosion will come, and start asking where they will be when it does. He is at home with his wife when the first strike hits nearby. The windows shudder. Dust falls from the ceiling. In the days that follow, the street outside fills with the sounds that later invade his sleep: sirens, shouted warnings, the uneven crack of distant gunfire. He describes the strange split of those days, in which part of him keeps functioning—buying bread, checking on neighbors, answering messages—while another part remains braced for impact.

The worst event happens when he is moving through the city during an errand, trying to get home before dark. He remembers a blast so sudden that there is no time to think, only the sensation of the ground jerking beneath him and then the hard, stunned silence afterward. He is not badly physically injured, but he sees people on the street injured and running, hears someone crying for a child, smells smoke and dust. He says that in that moment he understands, with a clarity that feels almost unreal, that the world can change in a second and that there is no promise of safety left. Afterward, he moves through the chaos in a narrow tunnel of action, searching for his wife, trying to call her, repeating her name in his head like a prayer.

From that day forward, fear becomes organized around the body. He begins scanning every environment automatically, measuring exits, checking ceilings, listening for engines or abrupt changes in sound. Loud noises make him jerk before he can stop himself. He avoids crowded places, not because he dislikes people, but because he cannot tolerate not knowing where to stand if something happens. He says he has become ashamed of how quickly his chest tightens and how his hands clench when a door slams or a car backfires. Even in safer settings later, his body behaves as though it is still in the war zone.

Sleep becomes one of the first casualties. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes sweating, sometimes after dreams in which he is trapped under debris, unable to find his wife or his way out of the city. When he wakes, he takes several seconds to remember where he is. The relief never lasts long. He often lies in the dark listening, trying to identify every sound in the building. During the day, images return without warning—smoke, the flash of the blast, faces of injured strangers—and he feels his stomach drop as if he is falling back into the scene. He hates these intrusions because they make him feel less like a man who survived and more like someone still trapped in it.

Dance, which once gave shape to his life, becomes complicated. He continues to move, but the ease is gone. He notices that sharp sounds during rehearsals make him lose concentration. He becomes tense when other dancers come too close from behind, and he startles if someone approaches suddenly. Sometimes he cannot remember sequences that he once knew instinctively, and he experiences this as humiliation. He works harder to hide it, smiling when he feels detached, pushing through performances with a fixed expression. The audience sees control; he feels himself monitoring every muscle, as if the stage is another place where danger might erupt.

He and his wife survive together, but he notices that he has become more withdrawn. He protects her from his fear by saying little, yet the silence between them grows heavier. He does not want to burden her with the images he carries, and he does not want her to see how often he checks doors or how easily he becomes irritable when startled. At times he feels guilty for having survived when others did not. At other times he feels numb, embarrassed by how little he seems able to feel except vigilance and fatigue. He describes himself as always “half there,” watching life from a slight distance, as if the part of him that once moved freely through the world has been left behind in the street where the blast happened.

Even now, months later, he still lives as though the next sound might split the air. He can function, work, and speak with composure, but the cost is constant effort. He is aware of how much of his day is spent managing his body’s alarms, and he is tired in a way that sleep does not repair.
